1:
The chapter opens a new subject, and they explain why it stands here. Matthew Henry compares the earlier prophet, who when he foretold the captivity added warnings against idolatry, both because the temptations of Babylon would draw the Jews there and because its afflictions were designed to cure them; so here the people are armed against heathen usages, that being reclaimed by the word they might be spared the rod. Adam Clarke gives the outline: the Jews about to be carried away are warned against the superstition of the country they are going to, after which the prophet exposes the absurdity of idolatry in a short but elegant satire, turning in a beautiful apostrophe to the one true God whose perfections he contrasts with the nothings the nations fear. Charles Ellicott finds the link with what precedes in the address itself: the house of Israel had just been told it was uncircumcised in heart and on a level with the heathen, and now the special sin it was disposed to follow is set out in words of scorn. John Calvin explains the preface as a necessity: the Jews had so hardened themselves in errors derived from the Gentiles that they could not easily be drawn away, and the prophet therefore begins with a formal summons to hear. John Gill weighs the preposition, which may mean unto you or upon you or concerning you.

The warning is directed at a particular superstition. Keil and Delitzsch render the command as a caution against using oneself to the ways of the heathen, and identify the ordinances named as their religious ideas and customs, whose vanity is proved by that of their gods. Clarke thinks the words addressed more particularly to the ten tribes scattered among the heathen, and perhaps to those left at home; he identifies the signs of heaven as the sun, moon, planets and constellations, or the figures representing them, and notes that the Chaldeans and Egyptians were notoriously addicted to astrology. John Wesley notes that judicial astrologers of whatever nation were generally called Chaldeans, and reads the last clause as leaving the practice to the heathen, since it does not become God’s people. Ellicott refers the signs to the astrologers and stargazers and monthly prognosticators named by the earlier prophet, who found portents in the conjunction of planets or in eclipses and comets; and he draws a contrast, that against the abject attitude such observation produces, what has been called in scorn an anthropomorphic theology was the one effectual safeguard against a superstition that bows before anything unusual and unexplained.

Calvin devotes most of his attention to two small words. He reports that the grammarians take the first as meaning according to, that one version turns the clause into conform ye not to the way of the heathen, and that it may be read as a simple negative; but he thinks it most probably a copying error for a particle this prophet writes elsewhere. On the particle introducing the last clause he sets out three expositions: that it means as, so that the sense is as the Gentiles are terrified; that it is adversative, meaning though; or that it gives a reason, so that it was absurd for the Jews to be terrified by celestial signs, having left that folly to the Gentiles whom God regarded as wholly blind. Henry draws the practical rule—do not approve the way of the heathen, nor think indifferently of it, much less imitate it, and do not let their customs steal in, as they are apt to do insensibly, or mingle with your religion; it ill becomes those taught of God to worship him with rites used in the worship of false gods. Gill notes that the ways meant are religious ways, many already learned and more in danger of being learned.
3:
The word rendered customs is given a narrower sense by everyone. Charles Ellicott prefers ordinances of the peoples, since the prophet is speaking not of common customs but of religious institutions, and of these as belonging not to Israel but to the nations round about. John Gill gives the alternatives—decrees or statutes, the determinations founded on observation of the stars, or the rites and ceremonies used in worshipping the host of heaven—and notes that the Syriac renders the clause the idols of the people are nothing. Adam Clarke takes the statutes and principles of the science as vain, empty and illusory, founded in ignorance and folly, and refers the ridicule of the following verses to two parallel passages in the earlier prophet. John Calvin asks why the prophet seems to break off, having warned against celestial signs and then passing at once to idols; the answer, he says, lies in the prestige of the nations concerned. The Jews were influenced by the ancient opinion that the Chaldeans and the Egyptians were alone wise, a reputation they had among all nations, since even heathen writers trace the origin of the sciences to them; the Jews allowed them so much authority that their minds, possessed by that prejudice, could discern nothing aright. The prophet therefore shakes off this stupidity by showing how foolish those were who would be thought alone wise and regarded others as barbarous. Calvin adds a note on the word itself, that it strictly means statutes, from a verb meaning to decree or write, and that though law is the general term this special one often occurs and is frequently applied to ceremonies and rites.

Ellicott raises a question of literary priority that the parallels force. The verses that follow are so closely parallel to three passages in the earlier prophet that the natural conclusion is that one writer had seen the work of the other; and the grandeur and fulness of that prophet’s language, together with the unlikeness of what stands here to this prophet’s usual style, makes it more probable that this is the copy—which so far adds to the argument for ascribing the other chapter to the earlier writer. He allows the possibility, entertained by some critics, that these verses are an interpolation, in which case they supply no evidence either way; but the fact that they are found in the Greek as well as the Hebrew tells in favour of their genuineness. He notes also that the substance of what follows has a parallel in the epistle ascribed to this prophet in an apocryphal book.

The making of the image is then described step by step. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the predicate has to be supplied in the third verse, since the sentence runs simply that it is wood which one has hewn out of the forest; the word for the tool they take, with a Jewish commentator, as an axe, suitably here since it must mean a carpenter’s implement, though the same word is doubtful in the parallel passage. The images, they add, were made of wood and covered with silver. Gill explains the purpose of the covering, that plates of silver and gold are laid on for ornament so that the thing may look grand and venerable and so draw the eye and the devotion of the people. Calvin presses the absurdity of the sequence: the workman takes the wood, polishes it by art, and then men think the result to be gods—a madness he calls detestable. The nailing that follows is noted by all as the completion of the process, the image being fastened so that it cannot move.
5:
The comparison in the fifth verse is the chapter’s hardest word, and Charles Ellicott sets out two quite different possibilities. The Hebrew word rendered upright has two meanings. On the first it means twisted, rounded or carved, and is commonly translated beaten work elsewhere; taken so, it refers to the twisted palm-like columns of a temple, to which the stiff formal figure of the idol—arms pressed to the side, with none of the action found in Greek statues—is compared. On the second, adopted by many commentators, it means a garden of gourds, and is so rendered in the earlier prophet. Ellicott notes that the comparison in the apocryphal epistle of an idol to a scarecrow in a garden of cucumbers shows the latter meaning was accepted when that epistle was written; on that view the idol was like the figures Greeks and Romans placed in gardens and orchards as scarecrows. Like figures, he adds, were used by another people of the region, and the practice seems to have been gaining ground even in Judah. John Gill and Adam Clarke both keep the received rendering, Gill explaining that the images are nailed to a post or set on a pedestal and so stand erect without bending, like the palm which is noted for uprightness—a sarcasm, he says, and a bitter one; Clarke puts it more shortly, that they are as straight and as stiff as the trees they were hewn from.

John Calvin uses the verse to state the borrowing openly. The prophet borrows his words from the forty-fourth chapter of his predecessor, the passage being wholly similar; being later, he took the words from him so that his own nation might be more impressed on finding the same thing said by two prophets, and so having two witnesses. On the fastening Calvin reports a reading that refers the last word to the metal, so that the pieces might not come off, but prefers the simpler sense that the statues were fixed by nails and hammers so that they might not be moved. He presses the absurdity as far as it will go: what could be more sottish than to think the nature of a tree changed as soon as it receives a new form, and that by the hand of an artificer? He observes that even heathen authors derided the folly, and quotes a Roman poet on a workman uncertain whether to make a bench or a garden idol of his timber. The design, Calvin says, is to remove a false notion: the wisdom of the Chaldeans and Egyptians so enraptured the Jews that they thought nothing came from those nations but what deserved esteem.

The turn to God in the sixth verse is deliberate, and Calvin explains why it comes here. The truth that the gods of the heathen are figments would be useless were the knowledge of the true God not added, since no one can know that gods of wood and stone are of no account unless the truth about God shines out first; whoever does not understand who God is can never be influenced by the doctrine that heathen superstitions are sacrilegious. The prophet therefore turns to the true God so that the brightness of his glory might dissipate the darkness the Gentiles were in, and so that by acknowledging one God men might not merely despise idols but abhor them. Ellicott finds the received opening a somewhat flat addition to the Hebrew, which begins with a vigorous abruptness, none is there like unto thee; and he notes that the phrase rendered great in might uses an almost technical word for the divine omnipotence. Gill lists the respects in which none is like God—the perfections of his nature, the works of his hands, and his kindness in grace and providence—and observes that there is none like him either for bestowing favours or for inflicting punishments.
7:
The question that opens the seventh verse is heard as indignation rather than inquiry. John Calvin calls it very emphatic, as though the prophet were rebuking the stupidity of all who did not acknowledge the only true God: whence is it that thou art not feared throughout the world? Were there a spark of right knowledge in men they would acknowledge him as the one God and submit to his power; when instead they invent various gods and every one is led here and there without judgment, the thing is monstrous. Even the rudest, when the subject is pressed on them, confess some supreme deity and are at length constrained to allow that there is but one true God—whence then the multitude and variety of gods in the world? How is it that those who hold the principle that God ought to be worshipped fall away and can never determine who he is or how he is to be worshipped? Calvin explains the title king of the nations as meaning not that the nations submitted to his authority but that he manifested evidences of his power everywhere, which might have induced the rudest to show him honour. John Gill makes the same distinction: not that the fear of him was general or that he was owned as their king, but that being their king of right he ought to have been feared, so that not to fear him was great stupidity and ingratitude. Charles Ellicott takes the title emphatically as king of the heathen, expressing the universal sovereignty of God against the thought that he was the God of the Jews only, and corrects the following clause to for it is thine—that is, the kingdom over the heathen implied in the title just given.

The comparison with the wise is pressed by all. Ellicott would omit the word men, since God is compared not with the sages of the heathen only but with all to whom they looked as sources of wisdom, and he prefers sovereignty to kingdoms in the parallel clause. Adam Clarke draws the conclusion from history: not even the wisest and most cultivated of the nations ever found out any one equal to God, but so exalted is he that in all their research they never found out the true God; and he notes that the fear of God is often taken for the whole of true religion. Keil and Delitzsch set out the contrast the passage is built on, that God is God in truth, the word truth standing strongly against vanity, and the living God against the dead gods just described, and everlasting king of the whole world, before whose wrath the earth trembles and the peoples quake.

The eighth verse gathers the whole indictment into a sentence, and its second clause is disputed. Gill weighs the first: they are altogether brutish, or one and all so, with not a wise man among them; or, on another rendering, in one thing they are brutish, namely in their idolatry, however wise they may be otherwise. Clarke reports a translation which turns the clause about the wood into a rebuke rather than a teaching—the wood itself is a rebuker of vanities—and explains the point, that the very tree out of which the god is hewn demonstrates the folly of the worshipper, since no art of man can make out of a log an animate and intelligent being. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received sense, that the teaching of the vanities is wood, so that the whole doctrine of the idols amounts to the material they are made of. The list of materials that follows completes the argument: silver beaten into plates and brought from far, gold from elsewhere, the work of craftsman and goldsmith, with blue and purple for clothing—every part of the god supplied by trade and finished by hire.
9:
The materials of the idol are traced to their sources, and the geography divides the commentators. On the first name Charles Ellicott takes it as elsewhere for Spain, from which the land was chiefly supplied with silver and tin through the traders of the coast. Adam Clarke reports the same supposition, that it is the port in Spain from which those traders brought much silver. John Calvin takes it instead for Cilicia, the transmarine country opposite Judea across the Mediterranean, and says the sea of that name is what they called the part extending toward Cilicia and Asia Minor. John Wesley makes it the proper name of a town in Cilicia which, being a noted port, is usually put for the ocean and may signify any place beyond the sea. John Gill canvasses more possibilities, that it was in Cilicia where the Apostle was born, or, as an earlier father reports one historian, a country in India; he notes that one version renders it Africa, and weighs the epithet applied to the silver—rolled up, or solid, or the best—preferring beaten into plates, since such plates could be rolled for shipment and used to deck the idols so that they might command awe from the common people.

The second name is more doubtful still. Ellicott calls it possibly an error of transcription or a dialectical variation for a name meaning the gold-coast, notes that the word occurs only here and in one other book, and reports that some interpreters connect it with the name of a tributary of the Indus; we cannot, he says, attain to greater certainty. Clarke reports one scholar’s identification with the river Pison and another view that a different gold-country is meant. Calvin rejects the suggestion that the word means pure or fine gold and holds it the name of a country east of Judea, Persia or somewhere near it. Wesley supposes simply that the best gold came from there as the best silver from the other place. On the colours, Ellicott identifies both as obtained from a Mediterranean shell-fish and used for the curtains of the tabernacle as well as for heathen idols, and cautions that purple in the English Bible means a deep crimson; Clarke calls them the most precious dyes, rare and of high price. Calvin explains why the pomp is described at all: he is anticipating an objection, since the world showed so much honour to idols precisely because their splendour dazzled men’s eyes, and the devil has always used this artifice; so the prophet grants the fact—the metals really are brought from far, really are melted and formed and polished—and calls the whole thing frivolous and extremely puerile.

Against all this the tenth verse sets three titles. Ellicott renders the first literally as the God that is Truth, and observes that the thought is the one for which a later writer uses a word meaning truth in its highest and most perfect form; on the last he says the English is not wrong but the Hebrew idiom, king of eternity, is far grander. Clarke insists the divine name be preserved however it is pronounced, and expounds the three in order: he is without beginning and without end, which is true of no other being; his being is underived and he gives life to all; and as he has made, so he governs all things, so that storms and earthquakes are the effects of his power and the overturning of nations the effect of his displeasure. Gill takes the first title either as opposed to all nominal and fictitious deities, which are gods only by name and in the foolish imagination of the people, or as meaning that the Lord God is truth—that cannot lie, is true to his covenant and promises, and will never deceive those who rely on him.
11:
The eleventh verse is the one unique thing in the book. Charles Ellicott calls it an almost unique phenomenon: the verse is not in Hebrew but in Aramaic, the language of the enemies of Israel. He gives two explanations. On the first, a marginal note added by one of the exiles found its way later into the text; on the second, which he thinks far more probable, the prophet, familiar with the Chaldean language, put into the mouths of his countrymen the answer they were to give when invited to join the worship of their conquerors—little as they knew of the strange tongue, they could learn enough for this. He adds that the words have the ring of a popular proverb, with a play of sound in the original barely reproducible in English, and suggests that the apocryphal epistle may be a rhetorical sermon on this text. Adam Clarke describes the dialect as a mixture of Hebrew, Syriac and Chaldee such as he supposes was spoken in Babylon during the captivity, the message being to the Babylonians and given in their own language. He reports that the Chaldee paraphrase makes it the beginning of a letter the prophet sent to the elders of the captivity, that all the ancient versions acknowledge the verse, and that it is found in every manuscript so far collated except one, whose editor enclosed it between lines as doubtful. He passes on a conjecture that a teacher during the captivity, deducing it from the prophet’s words, had it written in the margin and read with this section in the assemblies so that the people might have their answer ready when molested about their religion; another editor, he notes, leaves it out of the text entirely.

Keil and Delitzsch defend it against exactly that treatment. It must not be regarded as a gloss, they say, on the grounds urged by the several scholars they name—that it is in Chaldee, and that the tenth and twelfth verses connect directly. Neither the language nor the subject-matter favours that view; the content does not bear the character of a gloss, and no copyist would have interpolated a Chaldee verse into a Hebrew text. Besides, the verse is in the Greek version, and in point of sense it connects very suitably with what precedes: God is everlasting king, whereas the gods which did not make heaven and earth shall perish from under the heavens. They note that one word appears in a harder form than usual and that the last word of the verse is Hebrew and does not belong to the sentence. John Gill gives the plain account, that the godly Jews are to say this to the idolatrous Chaldeans, which is why this verse alone is written in that language. John Calvin presses the courage required: the Israelites are told to speak in Chaldee because they had been led into exile and mingled with their conquerors, and what is required of these despised exiles is a bold confession—though in the most miserable bondage and oppressed as slaves, they are to proclaim the glory of God in contempt of all the idols around them.

The twelfth verse returns to Hebrew and to creation. Ellicott notes that the verbs are participial, making and establishing, and complete the list of divine attributes begun two verses earlier; he distinguishes the word rendered world from the material earth, as the inhabited world in its relation to man, and prefers skill to discretion. Keil and Delitzsch mark a third section in which the power of the living God is shown from his government of nature, the overthrow of the false gods declared, and the Creator finally set forth as the God of Israel. Gill observes that the Chaldee paraphrase treats these words as a continuation of the answer the Jews are to give.
13:
The thirteenth verse turns from the settled order of creation to its changes, and John Calvin marks the distinction. There is in nature a perpetual constancy as to the heavens and the earth, and also many things subject to change—when God darkens the air, raises winds, pours down rain—which do not happen according to that settled order; so the prophet, having referred until now to the fixed government established at creation, sets before us things of another kind. Calvin prefers to render the disputed noun multitude or abundance rather than sound, and takes the voice for thunder: though it often rains without thunder, when God thunders from heaven there is a sudden change which not only disturbs the air but fills us with dread, and in that unexpected change the power of God more strikingly appears. On the rising vapours he concedes that natural philosophers show how it happens, but insists that the power of God is not excluded when we say a thing is done according to nature; the wonder is that vapours rise at a distance and immediately spread over our heads, and were we not accustomed to it we should be astonished. Adam Clarke supplies the chemistry of his own day, describing water as composed of two gases which the electric spark decomposes and which on recombining form water again, so that lightning acting on them produces rain; and he notes that this verse and the three following stand in substance and nearly in words in another chapter.

Charles Ellicott prefers a rush of waters to a multitude, following on the thunder which is thought of as the voice of God, and observes that the prophet finds tokens of almighty power alike in the fixed order of the world and in its most catastrophic disturbances; the strict construction of the Hebrew, he says, gives at the voice of his giving the roar of waters. He notes that the second half of the verse agrees verbally with a psalm, so that one is a quotation from the other or both from a common source, though we have no data for saying which is older. John Wesley states the structure plainly, that where the previous verse related God’s power in creating and fixing the stated order of things, this sets it forth in his providential ordering and disposing of them. John Gill glosses the uttered voice as God declaring his will and issuing his commands, or else as thunder.

The fourteenth verse turns the contrast back on the idol-maker. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a consequence: in the presence of such marvels of divine power and wisdom all men seem brutish and without knowledge, and all makers of idols are put to shame because of the image they make for a god, which is but a deception with no breath of life. They note that the word for the molten image properly means a drink-offering and is used here in the sense of a cast figure, as in three other books. On the phrase calling the idols a work of mockings they give two senses: either a work exposed to ridicule once the nullity of these supposed gods is brought to light, or, as two scholars take it, a work which makes mockery of its own worshippers and deludes them. Gill weighs the preposition in the first clause, so that a man is brutish either in his knowledge—that is, in the very science of making an idol, whether of wood or of gold or brass, if he thinks that having made it he has made a god—or else because of knowledge, meaning for want of it, since being without the knowledge of God he is like the beasts that perish.
15:
Two words in the fifteenth verse are disputed, and both bear on who is being condemned. John Calvin notes that what was called falsehood before is now called vanity: the earlier word meant that men were grossly deceived when they sought the presence of God in dead things, and the second adds that the idols are empty. On the second phrase he refuses the sense many give it. Some render it mockeries, taking the word passively, and one ancient paraphrase makes it a thing worthy of ridicule and laughter, several versions agreeing; but Calvin says the word means no such thing, since the verb behind it means to wander or go astray, and in its causative form to lead astray or deceive. He takes the noun as referring to persons rather than as an abstract, so that the line runs: vanity are they, the work of the grossly deluded—the threat that follows falling not on the idols only, as before, but on their makers. He prefers imposture or deception to mockery, and supports the sense from the patriarch’s fear of being found out by his father as one acting in guile. Charles Ellicott takes it the other way, preferring a work of mockery—worthy of that and of that only—and suggesting that the word was substituted, after this prophet’s manner, for a technical term not unlike it in sound which elsewhere means image work. He glosses the time of their visitation as the time when they are visited with punishment. John Wesley dates that visitation historically, as when God comes to reckon with Babylon and her idols. John Gill takes the vanity as showing the emptiness of the human mind that worships such things and their uselessness as objects of trust.

The sixteenth verse answers all of it with a single contrasting phrase. Keil and Delitzsch explain the expression from the law: sun, moon and stars were apportioned to the nations as gods, while Israel was taken to be a people of inheritance, so that the God who fell to Jacob’s lot as his inheritance is quite other than these. They gloss the reason given—he is the framer of the universe—and take the second title to mean the race which belongs to him as a peculiar possession, comparing three other passages where similar phrases are used of the people, of a mountain, and of the godly servants of the Lord. Adam Clarke sets the contrast in its ancient context: every nation had its tutelary god, and that was its portion, the division of the heavenly bodies among the nations being expressly stated in the law, while the Lord took Israel to be his portion; he cites the psalmist calling the Lord the portion of his inheritance, and notes that the earlier prophet uses the same word ironically of the smooth stones of the brook to which idolaters paid divine honours. The whole force of the verse, he says, lies in the last clause: the God of Jacob is not like them, for he is the former of all things, whereas they are formed by their foolish worshippers. Gill draws the same comparison out at length, that there is no portion so large or so rich or so satisfying or so durable, since God is the portion of his people in all the perfections of his nature and in all his persons, and all that he has is theirs both now and hereafter.
17:
The long argument against idols now breaks off and the threat resumes. Charles Ellicott marks the structure: the section just closed had been a long parenthesis reproving Israel for the sin that placed it among the uncircumcised in heart, and the prophet now returns to his main theme, the devastation of the land as the penalty of that sin. He begins with a vivid touch in a picture of utter misery—the daughter of Israel, the word for inhabitant being feminine, sitting as in a besieged fortress, is to gather her goods into one small bundle and go into exile with that as her sole remnant. He objects to the English wares as suggesting trade, which is foreign to the context, and thinks the word may mean simply the travelling carpet or mantle the exile was to take with him; the whole phrase, he adds, has something of a proverbial type, like a Roman satirist’s take up your packages and begone. John Gill gives the more commercial sense, that the Jews were to gather their valuables from the several parts of the country and bring them to the fortified city, or be in danger of losing them to the enemy; he reports a Jewish commentator who reads the verse as spoken to the Chaldeans instead, telling them not to be elated at the captivity of Israel. John Calvin rejects that reading firmly. The rabbinic interpreters take the first verse of the Chaldeans, which he thinks very incorrect, since the whole preceding argument was meant to confirm the Israelites in captivity; and it is strange, he says, that they apply the second verse to the Israelites while reading the first by itself, as though the two were unconnected. Adam Clarke and John Wesley both keep the simple sense, that the people are to pack up what necessaries their enemies will permit them to carry away, the fortress meaning the inhabitants of Jerusalem as the chief place of security in the land.

Matthew Henry explains why the warning was needed. The Jews who remained after some were carried off were very secure, thinking themselves inhabitants of a fortress and their country an impregnable stronghold; they are here told to think of leaving it and to contract their affairs into as small a compass as they can, since this is not their rest. Calvin gives the same reason—the country would be exposed to plunder, so that with devastation at hand the prophet bids those in fortified places gather their goods—and adds an observation on the manner: the prophets ironically touch the torpidity of the people, since plain truth would have had no effect unless urged vehemently, and the prophet here takes the character of a man bringing warlike tidings. The point of it all, he says, is that nowhere in Judea would there be safety.

The eighteenth verse gives the reason, and the figure in it is pressed by everyone. Keil and Delitzsch render it as hurling forth the inhabitants of the land this time, and pressing them hard. Henry works the same image out: they had hitherto dropped out a few at a time, but one captivity more shall make a thorough riddance, and they shall be slung out as a stone from a sling—so easily and so thoroughly, thrown out with violence and driven to a place a great distance off, with nothing of them remaining. He notes the same comparison used elsewhere for an utter destruction, and finds a second threat in the words that follow: God will not only throw them out, which he might do while they remained easy elsewhere, but will distress them, that they may find it so. Gill observes only that the verse gives the reason enforcing the exhortation before it, and shows that the same people are addressed in both.
19:
From this point the chapter is spoken in the first person, and the commentators agree on who is speaking. Charles Ellicott says that from here to the end we have, with this prophet’s dramatic vividness, the lamentation of the daughter of Israel in captivity, bewailing the transgressions that led to it; its following immediately on the previous verse supports reading the earlier phrase as meaning that Israel has found her punishment in both senses. John Wesley says the same briefly, that the prophet here personates the complaint of the people of the land. John Calvin explains the device at length. The prophet speaks in the name of the whole people because no one was moved by threatenings however grievous; the manner is common to all the prophets, who first address the people and then, producing no effect, speak of themselves as in God’s presence to rebuke the hardness of their hearers. He did not grieve on his own account but represents the grief the people ought to have felt and did not, so that the words describe not their feeling but their duty—were there a particle of wisdom in them they would bewail the calamity before judgment fell, but no one is moved, and so, in effect, I shall weep alone, and it is on your account.

The words of the lament are then glossed. John Gill takes the hurt as the breach made on the Jews when besieged and carried captive, with which the prophet heartily sympathised, considering their calamities as his own. Ellicott renders the second word as meaning all but incurable, and prefers this is my grief or plague—that which I have brought upon myself and must therefore bear; to accept the punishment was in this, as in all cases, the first step to reformation. Adam Clarke puts the same submission in the speaker’s mouth: oppressive as it is, I have deserved it and worse, yet even in this judgment God remembers mercy.

The figure of the ruined tent is the chapter’s most affecting image, and its point is disputed only in detail. Ellicott sets out the whole: the tent which had been the home of Israel is destroyed, the cords that fastened it to the ground are broken, and the children who used to help their mother arrange the tent and its curtains are not—that is, are either dead or in exile. There is something significant, he observes, in the destruction of a city being represented under the imagery of a tent, since the daughter of Zion has as it were been brought back to her nomadic state. Calvin thinks the metaphor may be taken from shepherds, suiting the next verse, though the prophets often compare the church to a tent for another reason: though it is said elsewhere to be built on the holy mountains, as to its external condition it may justly be called a tent, since there is no fixed residence for God’s children on earth and they are often constrained to change their place. He rejects the view that the tent means the city as strained and unsuitable, holding rather that the people are compared to a man dwelling with his family in a tent; the complaint is that they were deprived of all their children and, worse than if these had been taken by death, that they were scattered here and there, with no one left to bring them assistance in their want. Wesley describes the mechanics of the image, that the cords fasten the tent on every side to stakes in the ground, so that when they are broken the tent falls. Gill weighs whether the tabernacle means the temple, or, as two ancient authorities have it, the city or the whole land, and inclines away from the temple. Clarke states it as the plain fact behind the figure, that the city is taken and the villages ruined and desolate.
21:
The cause of the disaster is laid at the door of the rulers, and the only question is how wide the word reaches. John Gill reports that three Jewish authorities confine the shepherds to the kings of Judah, naming two of them, but thinks it need not be so restricted, since it may include all inferior civil magistrates and even all ecclesiastical rulers, who were the shepherds of the people; being like brute beasts and without understanding of civil or religious things, they were the cause of the ruin. Adam Clarke narrows it again to the king and his counsellors, who by refusing to pay the promised tribute had kindled a new war. Charles Ellicott takes the word as used elsewhere in the book of rulers generally rather than of priests as such. John Calvin agrees with the wider sense and gives his reason: he includes the priests and prophets as well as the king and his counsellors, and explains that the prophet did not mean to exempt the people from fault but to name the origin and primary cause of the evils, since kings and prophets and priests being blind, the flock of God was destroyed. He adds why the prophets so often single out the great: it mostly happens that those in humble stations rely much on the chief men who hold authority, so that the evil had to be noticed; and there is besides so much pride in kings and priests and in all who enjoy honour, who think themselves exempt from the restraint of laws and refuse to be reproved as though they were sacred persons, that such men had to be rebuked with vehemence. Calvin observes that the people of that time repudiated the prophets by pleading the authority of their bishops and kings, and applies the same complaint to the church of his own day; the argument is reported here, but not the polemic it is wrapped in.

One phrase in the verse is corrected. Ellicott prefers therefore they have not done wisely to therefore they shall not prosper, since acting wisely is the primary meaning of the word and prosperity only its secondary sense as the result of prudence, and he notes that the Greek, the Latin and most other versions take it so. He also renders the last words literally as all their pasture, the place or the act of pasturing, taken practically for the sheep that fed there.

The rumour of the invader closes the section. Gill identifies it as the report that the king of Babylon had invaded the land and was coming up to besiege Jerusalem, and the commotion out of the north as a large army from a country lying north of Judea, coming with great noise and causing trembling among the inhabitants. Clarke gives the same sense and objects to the English: he cannot imagine how the word bruit got into the version, and offers a plain rendering—the voice of the report, behold it is come, and great commotion from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a habitation of wild beasts. The meaning, he says, is that the report of an intended invasion is now confirmed: the invader has entered the land, the enemy is at the doors, and the total desolation of Judah is their sole object. Keil and Delitzsch render the opening as an exclamation, hark, a rumour, behold it comes, and translate the last words as an abode of jackals rather than of dragons.
23:
The closing prayer opens with a confession about human agency. John Gill reports two Jewish commentators who apply it to the Babylonian king: setting out from Babylon he intended to march against the Ammonites, but where two roads met God changed his mind and turned him toward Jerusalem. Gill thinks the words more general, that none of the godly could escape the coming judgments, being entirely in God’s hands. John Calvin reports the same tradition referred to an earlier Assyrian king, and calls it frivolous; he refers the words to the Jews themselves, who had long dismissed all fear as though their own counsels could secure the public good, and who when the prophets denounced vengeance regarded only their present state, as though God could not in one instant vibrate his lightnings from the rising to the setting sun. He gives the verse literally—not to a mortal is his way, nor for man to walk and establish his steps. Charles Ellicott says the confession is made not by the prophet for himself but for Israel, and observes that the two Hebrew words for man in the two clauses express the weakness and the strength of men, so that even the strong man must confess he needs a hand other than his own to direct his steps. Adam Clarke hears a refusal to dispute: God does everything wisely, they have sinned and he has a right to punish and to choose the punishment. John Wesley makes it the ground of what follows, that it is not in their power to divert these judgments, though God can moderate them.

The petition asks for measure, not exemption. Ellicott calls the received rendering accurate but prefers the translation used elsewhere in the book, in measure, the discipline that comes from God as righteous Judge—at once retributive and reformative—being contrasted with punishment that is simply vindictive. Gill takes the speaker as representing the nation and especially the godly, who do not refuse correction, knowing a father’s chastisements are for good, but ask that it be in measure and so as to make a difference between God’s people and others. Clarke and Wesley say the same briefly: the punishment should not be to the uttermost of the offence, since in the midst of judgment God is asked to remember mercy. Calvin draws a hard inference from the form of the request. The prophet personates the whole people and shows how they must have felt had they not been blinded, so that the only thing left them was to ask pardon suppliantly—not refusing chastisement altogether but supplicating forgiveness only in part, that God would not exercise such severity as to consume them. This shows how atrocious their sins were: one who sins lightly may flee to God’s mercy and say, forgive me, but those who have accumulated evils and not repented after many warnings can ask only that the vengeance be moderated.

The last verse turns the prayer outward. Gill reads it as asking God to make a difference, correcting his own people in measure while pouring out fury on those ignorant of him. Clarke states the argument behind it—if judgment begins at the house of God, those who never acknowledged him cannot escape—and traces its fulfilment in the fate of the Babylonian kings and the capture of the city; he then turns the verse against households where the worship of God is not maintained, and asks what blessing such a family can expect. Keil and Delitzsch set out the verse as the close of the entreaty. Ellicott notes that the words are identical with those of a psalm and thinks it more probable that the psalmist borrowed from the prophet, though many critics date that psalm much later and its own language suggests it is at any rate later than the destruction of the temple, on which supposition the two writers may have been contemporaries.
